summaries.example: Imagine a town leader who tells everyone, “Please help clean the park.” One view says helping becomes a duty because the leader gave an order. Another says it becomes a duty because the leader wanted people to help. Philosophers ask whether moral duties work in a similar way with God’s commands or wishes. They also ask whether goodness and fairness would still matter in deciding what God would command.
summaries.summary: Theological voluntarism is a family of views about how God’s will may be connected to morality. Some versions are normative: they say that certain actions really are required because God commands or wills them. Other versions are metaethical: they try to explain the meaning or nature of moral ideas, such as obligation, by connecting them with divine commands or intentions. This second kind does not automatically say that any obligations exist. The view can be held by a theist, an atheist, or an agnostic, and it can be combined with moral skepticism. Philosophers must decide which moral ideas depend on God’s will, which divine act matters, and what “depend” means. They also debate whether God’s commands or intentions would make morality authoritative, non-random, and genuinely good. The entry presents these arguments as unsettled philosophical questions rather than as questions with one agreed answer.
key_ideas: Theological voluntarism connects at least some moral facts to God’s will.
A normative version says that people really have certain duties because of God’s will.
A metaethical version explains what moral ideas or properties are, without claiming that any duties actually exist.
A person could study or accept the metaethical view even if they were unsure that God exists or unsure that moral duties exist.
Philosophers disagree about whether duties depend on God’s commands, God’s intentions, or another act of will.
Important worries include whether morality would become random and whether this view can explain why God is good.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic asks a basic question about morality: where do duties come from, and what makes them binding? It also shows how philosophers separate two questions: what moral words mean and whether moral duties really exist. Studying the debate helps us understand how beliefs about God, authority, reasons, goodness, and fairness can fit together—or come apart.

important_terms.definition: The idea that some moral facts, such as what is required, depend on something God wills, such as a command or intention.
The study of what moral words and facts mean, such as “right,” “wrong,” or “required.”
A rule about what people should do. It says that some action is required, allowed, or forbidden.
A person who doubts or withholds judgment about whether any real moral requirements exist.

questions_to_think_about: Is something a duty because a trusted authority says so, or must there be another reason?
Could someone discuss what “duty” means while still being unsure whether any duties exist?
Would a command be fair if it had no good reason behind it?
What might make a person a real moral authority?

summaries.example: Suppose a ruler tells citizens to perform a difficult task. One theory says the task is obligatory because the ruler issued a genuine demand. A second says it is obligatory because the ruler antecedently intends that citizens perform it, even if no command is given. A third says the ruler’s willing that the task be obligatory directly causes its obligatory status. The analogy highlights the central choices in theological voluntarism, while also raising questions about authority: does a command create a reason, merely cause a duty, or express a reason that already exists?
summaries.summary: Theological voluntarism is the general thesis that some evaluative status is present in virtue of an act of divine will. The entry separates two forms. Normative theological voluntarism maintains that some normative state of affairs actually obtains—for example, that obedience to God is obligatory. Metaethical theological voluntarism instead offers an account of moral concepts, properties, or states of affairs in terms of divine willing; it does not by itself affirm that any obligation exists. Consequently, metaethical voluntarism is compatible with theism, atheism, agnosticism, and moral skepticism, whereas normative voluntarism is not compatible with skepticism about all normative states of affairs. The central formulation is open-ended: an evaluative status M stands in a dependence relation D to a divine act A. Philosophers therefore debate whether the relevant statuses are mainly obligation-family properties or all moral properties; whether the act is a command, an antecedent intention, or a direct willing that an obligation obtain; and whether dependence is analysis, reduction, supervenience, or causation. Arguments in favor appeal to the theological centrality of God, the historical relationship between moral and religious concepts, and the possibility that divine will explains morality’s unusual normativity, impartiality, overridingness, and content. Objections ask whether the theory makes God’s goodness circular or insubstantial, whether it makes morality arbitrary, and whether obligation is sufficiently different from other normative properties to receive a special theological explanation. The entry presents these issues as continuing disputes.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes normative theological voluntarism from metaethical theological voluntarism. The former affirms at least one obligation; the latter may remain compatible with moral skepticism.
Metaethical theological voluntarism can be formulated as a dependence claim: an evaluative status depends on a divine act, with the relevant status, act, and dependence relation left open for debate.

Defenders appeal to historical links between moral and theological concepts, claims about divine freedom or sovereignty, and the possibility that divine will explains morality’s normativity, impartiality, overriding force, or content.

A major dispute concerns whether obligation depends on divine commands or on divine intentions. A third proposal treats God’s willing an obligation as the direct cause, but the entry argues that this option is not clearly a rival to the others and lacks strong support in its strongest form.

Another debate concerns scope. A restricted view explains obligation-type properties through divine will while leaving goodness or virtue to another account; an unrestricted view extends the explanation to all moral statuses.

The principal objections concern God’s goodness, the alleged arbitrariness of morality, and whether the restricted view is sufficiently motivated. The entry reports plausible replies but no final resolution.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate concerns the metaphysical and practical foundations of morality. It asks whether moral requirements are independent truths, divine commands, divine intentions, or facts that depend on divine will in some other way. It also clarifies the difference between explaining what a moral concept means and asserting that moral obligations exist. Because the proposed dependence relations have different implications for reasons, authority, accountability, and moral knowledge, the issue is not merely about religious vocabulary; it is about what could make moral demands binding and intelligible.

important_terms.definition: A metaethical or normative position holding that some evaluative status depends on an act of divine will.
The branch of ethics that studies moral concepts, properties, reasons, and states of affairs rather than simply stating what one ought to do.
A view that asserts that some normative state of affairs actually obtains, such as an obligation to obey God.
A view about what moral concepts or properties are, possibly without affirming that any obligations exist.
The status of being required, permitted, or right in the conduct-guiding sense; much of the debate focuses on this family of statuses.
The relation by which one fact or property depends on another; proposed versions include analysis, reduction, supervenience, and causation.
A person who denies or suspends judgment about whether any normative state of affairs obtains.
A kind of authority whose directives help constitute another person’s reasons for action, rather than merely influencing them causally.

questions_to_think_about: If moral obligation is identical with, constituted by, or caused by a divine command, which of those relations best explains authority?
Can a person be a moral skeptic while endorsing a metaethical account that makes obligations depend on divine acts?
Does restricting theological voluntarism to obligation avoid the problem of explaining God’s goodness, or does it merely relocate the problem?
Must every basic moral fact be necessary or justified by another moral fact, or could it depend on a contingent nonmoral fact together with a necessary connection?
If divine commands are not wholly determined by reasons, does that make morality arbitrary, or can limited discretion be acceptable?

summaries.example: A school club president says, “Everyone must bring supplies tomorrow.” One student thinks the duty comes from the president’s spoken command. Another thinks it comes from the president’s plan that everyone bring supplies, even if the plan was never announced. A third student thinks the duty is whatever the president directly decides should be a duty. Philosophers use questions like these to examine whether moral obligations depend on God’s commands, intentions, or decisions—and whether a command must also have a good reason.
summaries.summary: Theological voluntarism concerns the relationship between divine will and moral status. Its normative form says that some duties or other normative facts actually hold because of divine commands or intentions. Its metaethical form is more cautious: it tries to explain moral concepts or properties through divine will without automatically asserting that obligations exist. This distinction allows metaethical voluntarism to be combined with atheism, agnosticism, or moral skepticism. The philosophical position is not one single formula. It may cover only obligation-like statuses, such as being required or permissible, or it may try to cover all moral statuses, including goodness and virtue. It may say that God commands an action, intends that it happen, or wills that the action be obligatory. It must also explain the kind of connection involved: perhaps the connection is part of the meaning of “obligatory,” an identity between obligation and divine command, a dependence relation, or a causal relation. Arguments for the position appeal to the importance of God in theistic ethics and to the possibility that divine will explains morality’s authority, impartiality, force, and content. Objections focus on whether morality would be arbitrary, whether God’s goodness could be explained without circularity, and whether obligation is truly special enough to depend on divine will while other moral ideas do not. The disputes remain open.
key_ideas: Theological voluntarism is broader than the label “divine command theory,” because some versions appeal to divine intentions or other acts of will rather than commands.
A normative view says that at least one duty exists. A metaethical view can instead discuss the nature of obligation while remaining unsure whether any obligation exists.
The view does not require the person considering it to be a theist. It can also be combined with atheism, agnosticism, or moral skepticism when the view is metaethical.
Supporters argue that divine will might explain why morality is binding on everyone, why it is impartial, and why moral demands concern the well-being or respect owed to beings.
Philosophers disagree about whether all moral properties depend on divine will or mainly properties such as required, permissible, and right.

Critics ask whether this makes morality arbitrary, whether it weakens the idea that God is good, and whether the theory has enough special support to explain obligation rather than morality in general.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate connects everyday questions about rules and authority with deep questions about the nature of morality. It asks whether moral duties are independent standards, results of divine decisions, or concepts rooted in a relationship with a divine authority. It also teaches an important philosophical habit: separate a claim about what morality means from a claim that moral facts exist. That distinction makes room for more positions than a simple choice between “God gives the rules” and “God has nothing to do with morality.”

important_terms.definition: A family of views saying that some moral or evaluative status depends on what God wills.
The study of what moral ideas mean and what moral properties or facts are, rather than only asking which actions to choose.
A view claiming that certain actions really are required because of divine will.
A view explaining moral concepts or properties through divine will, without necessarily claiming that any duties exist.
A moral status involving what someone must do, may do, or is forbidden to do.
The act of giving an authoritative instruction, such as telling someone that an action must be performed.
A settled aim or plan to bring about an action or state of affairs; some versions connect obligation to this rather than to an expressed command.
A view that doubts or suspends judgment about whether any moral requirements actually exist.

questions_to_think_about: Would an unspoken intention create a duty, or is an expressed command necessary?
Can an explanation of the meaning of “obligation” be true even if no one believes that God exists?
Why might someone think that duties are more closely connected to authority than virtues are?
If God has reasons for commands, do those reasons come from outside divine will or from another part of morality?
Does a rule become fair simply because a powerful authority chooses it?
